atlas-canvas.js is Atlas's pre-built diagram-js bundle. It carries both canvases
Atlas draws with, namespaced, under the global AtlasCanvas:

  - AtlasCanvas.archimate — the ArchiMate 3.2 canvas (ADR-0189): the Open Group
    Model Exchange parser, the renderer, and the authoring behaviour loaded on top
    when the caller may edit. Source: src/archimate.js
  - AtlasCanvas.uml — the three UML canvases (ADR-0237, ADR-0259). ClassCanvas draws the
    information model: the renderer and the subset-driven rules provider, editable
    because the model is a working copy with an explicit Save. ObjectCanvas draws
    one instance's object diagram — the run-time twin, read-only because the graph
    is derived by the server and has no document to write back to. StateCanvas draws
    a class's lifecycle — the states a business object moves through, and what a BPMN
    data state resolves against — authored like the class model and held to the rules
    the server serves beside the relationship matrix.
    Source: src/uml.js

  - diagram-js@15.26.0, once, for both of them

They were vendored as two bundles at first, a copy of diagram-js each, because the
UML canvas arrived later and merging them then would have meant touching Panorama's
shipped canvas for a saving that was real but not urgent. ADR-0237 named the merge
as the follow-up; this file is the result of it. 123,109 bytes where the two were
211,888 — 88,779 fewer, and one cache entry rather than two.

The two canvases share the library and nothing else. Each keeps its own renderer,
its own rules, and its own idea of what a document is: an ArchiMate view is read
from a server that owns it and is never created by the canvas, while an information
model is a working copy with an explicit Save, which is what makes an undo stack
mean anything. That is why they are namespaced rather than flattened into one
export list — Viewer and ClassCanvas in one namespace would read as two kinds of
the same thing, and they are not.

The editing modules (modeling, move, resize, outline, rules) are part of the bundle
whether or not a given canvas loads them. They are instantiated only for an editable
canvas, so a reader's diagram carries no modeling behaviour — but the code ships
either way, because a single buildless bundle is the whole point of vendoring it
(ADR-0012). The object canvas is the clearest case: it loads a renderer, selection,
pan and zoom and nothing else, because a derived picture has no document to edit.

Adding that third notation cost 4,476 bytes — 123,109 to 127,585 — which is the
same arithmetic the merge above rests on. One copy of diagram-js is the expensive
part and it is already paid for; a renderer is cheap.

Two more of the library's own modules joined later, and they are the exception to
that arithmetic because they are library rather than renderer: the palette — the one
bpmn-js and dmn-js put down their left edge, whose stylesheet was already sitting in
diagram-js.css unused — and ManhattanLayout, which bends a relationship into right
angles instead of drawing it straight through whatever lies between its ends.
Together 127,585 to 154,041, which is 26,456 bytes. Both replace something Atlas
would otherwise have written and then maintained: a hand-rolled toolbox that looked
like neither of the two canvases beside it, and a router that did not route.

The state canvas is the third notation and cost 6,888 bytes — 154,041 to 160,929 —
which is the renderer arithmetic again rather than the library's: a rounded box, an
arrow marker, and the one rule that nothing leaves a final state. Its run-time
overlay (ADR-0259 §4) cost 358 more — 160,929 to 161,287 — because it is marks on
that same notation and not a fourth one: a state a datum has been through is still
that state, so what it took was two class names and a label.

The line from a class to the enumeration its states come from cost 367 more —
161,287 to 161,654. It is not a fourth notation either: it is the store link's
construction pointed at a different pair, so what it took was an open arrowhead, a
keyword, and one more derived edge in the reconcile.

There is still a separate copy of diagram-js inside the vendored bpmn-js and dmn-js
bundles. Those are third-party bundles vendored whole rather than Atlas sources
built against the library, so folding them in would mean building bpmn-js from
source — a different decision from this one, and not one this merge makes.

diagram-js and its bundled dependencies are MIT licensed (see LICENSE). The Atlas
parsers, renderers and rules remain part of Atlas. Only the output is loaded at
runtime: Atlas remains a single, buildless, offline-capable binary.

Do not edit atlas-canvas.js by hand. To rebuild:

  npm install --no-save --no-package-lock diagram-js@15.26.0 esbuild@0.25.9
  npx esbuild api/web/vendor/canvas/src/index.js --bundle --format=iife \
    --global-name=AtlasCanvas --minify --legal-comments=none \
    --outfile=api/web/vendor/canvas/atlas-canvas.js
  cp node_modules/diagram-js/assets/diagram-js.css \
    api/web/vendor/canvas/diagram-js.css

SHA-256 atlas-canvas.js:
